title: VC0-03128
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Ghana, fears gender-based violence and persecution from her husband.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant was a genuine witness when it came to testifying about her life and circumstances following the death of her parents in 2014 but not credible with respect to her testimony about seeking police protection, her benefactor and the risk posed by her husband in the internal flight alternative (IFA). The RPD concluded that the Appellant has viable IFA in Accra.

Following my own review, I find that IFA is the determinative issue. The Appellant has not met her burden of proof to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility she would be persecuted or face a risk of harm in Accra or that it would be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances for her to seek refuge there.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

According to her Basis of Claim (BOC) form1 the Appellant was born in XXXX XXXX A year after the death of her parents in 2014, the Appellant was forced by her grandmother to marry the chief of their village, XXXX XXXXa XXXX XXXXyear-old man with four other wives and 17 children.

The Appellant's husband wanted to circumcise her and subjected her to sexual assaults, violence and intimidation. She had two miscarriages, lost her hearing in her right ear and has recurring pain in her left ear due to his assaults.
In 2016 the Appellant attempted to escape to neighbouring Togo, but her husband found her and brought her back the next day. He threatened to kill her if she attempted to flee again.

The Appellant tried to get help from the police on several occasions, but they told her they would not interfere in a marital relationship. Her husband is the village chief, is powerful and has many connections and is friends with the police and the village leaders. The police would not make any reports or records of the Appellant's complaints about her husband's abuse.

In XXXX 2019 the Appellant's husband left the village to attend a funeral and the Appellant fled to Accra where her benefactor arranged for somewhere to stay and facilitated her trip to Canada. The Appellant stayed in Accra until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, when she flew to Canada. Her claim for refugee protection was received on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts deference.2 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.
The determinative issue on this appeal is whether the RPD was correct when it found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Accra.
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred and that she does not have an IFA in Accra.

I have reviewed the evidence on the record, including the transcript of the RPD hearing and assessed the Appellant's submissions. As detailed below, I find that the RPD did not err and the Appellant has a viable IFA in Accra. Internal flight alternative

It is settled law that the concept of an IFA is an inherent part of the Convention refugee definition because a claimant must be a refugee from a country, not from a particular region of a country.3 The existence of an IFA is fatal to any refugee claim4 as recently confirmed in a 2020 decision of the Federal Court: The concept of an IFA is an inherent part of the definition of Convention refugee: see Valasquez v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1201 at para 15. If it is objectively reasonable for a claimant to live elsewhere in their country of nationality without fear of persecution, the claimant is not a Convention refugee, even if they have a well-founded fear of persecution in another part of the country.5

The test for assessing an IFA was set out in a recent decision of the Federal Court:6 To determine if a viable IFA exists, the RAD must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that (1) the claimant will not be subject to persecution (on a "serious possibility" standard), or a section 97 danger or risk (on a "more likely than not" standard) in the proposed IFA; and (2) in all the circumstances, including circumstances particular to the claimant, conditions in the IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there: Thirunavukkarasu at pp 595-597; Hamdan v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2017 FC 643 at paras 10-12. Both of these "prongs" of the test must be satisfied to conclude that a refugee claimant has a viable IFA. The threshold on the second prong of the IFA test is a high one. There must be "actual and concrete evidence" of conditions that would jeopardize the applicants' lives and safety in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area: Ranganathan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2000 CanLII 16789 (FCA), [2001] 2 FC 164 (CA) at para 15. Once the potential for an IFA is raised, the claimant bears the onus of establishing it is not viable: Thirunavukkarasu at pp 594-595.

The RPD complied with the procedural requirements to raise an IFA before or during the hearing. The RPD identified Accra as an IFA. Both the RPD7 and Appellant's counsel8 canvassed the viability of Accra as an IFA and Appellant's counsel made detailed submissions on both prongs of the IFA test.9 First prong of the IFA test: no serious possibility of persecution or not likely that the Appellant would face a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA

When the RPD asked the Appellant what she thought would happen if they were to return to Ghana, she gave the following testimony:10 Appellant: My husband will kidnap me and accuse me more and he might end up killing me, because he threatened to kill me once before. RPD: Why do you think he would be still interested in finding you? Appellant: Because of his reputation, because of his dignity. It is a shame on him that his wife has left him, runaway. So, he feels that disgracing. So, my life is really in danger if I go back to him. RPD: If you return to Ghana and remained in Accra, how would he be able to find you do you think? Appellant: He will find me because our people in the community are all over everywhere. So, they know that the chief's wife is not there. So, they will find me. RPD: So, the people from your village are everywhere or when you say people are everywhere? Appellant: Yes. People from my village travel to Accra too. So, they will know about me and they can tell him about me. RPD: How would they come to know about you in Accra, these people, just by chance? Appellant: Yeah, because they will see me, because they travel too. So, they will see me and all.

The RPD found that the Appellant did not present sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to determine that there is more than a mere possibility that she would be persecuted or risk harm in Accra citing a number of reasons, including: * Accra is the capital of Ghana with an urban population of 2.27 million.11 The Appellant returning to Accra would raise little suspicion compared to returning to the small village where her ex-husband is the traditional chief, which is in the Northern district over 600 km from Accra, which is almost 12 hours by car and considerably longer by public transport;12 * The Appellant lived with a friend without issue in Accra for three months. Although she testified that she feared for her safety, she encountered no issues and had no proof that her husband was looking for her;13 * The Appellant's single agent of harm is a tribal chief who supports himself through real estate in a village in Northern Ghana with approximately 4000 residents; * The Appellant provided almost no details as to how her agent of harm would be capable of finding her given the distance and relatively small size of the village and his limited profile in terms of influence and capacity.

The Appellant submits that the RPD's conclusion that her agent of harm does not have the ability to follow the Appellant to Accra is not supported by her testimony that she was followed by her husband to Togo. The Appellant argues that since there is no adverse finding that this did not occur, it is sufficient evidence of the ability of her husband to locate her anywhere in Ghana including Accra and that he threatened her with harm if she ever tried to leave him again.

I find that the RPD addressed the Appellant's attempted escape to Togo. The RPD found that the Appellant's escape to Togo was thwarted when her confidant told her husband about her whereabouts. The Appellant testified that she has no further connections with her community and is not in contact with her grandmother.14 "It would be reasonable that in returning to Ghana [the Appellant] would continue to no longer have contact with these persons that hold allegiance to her ex-husband."15

I find that the Appellant has not credibly demonstrated the influence, connections or motivation of her agent of persecution to either find out she returned to Ghana or to track her in Accra and she has not met her burden to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that she will be subject to persecution (on a "serious possibility" standard), or a section 97 danger or risk (on a "more likely than not" standard) in Accra. Second prong of the IFA test: it is not objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for the Appellant to relocate to the proposed IFA

The issue is whether it would be reasonable, in all the Appellant's circumstances, for her to relocate to Accra. As a starting point, the Federal Court of Appeal has held that there is: ...a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area. In addition, it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions. The absence of relatives in a safe place, whether taken alone or in conjunction with other factors, can only amount to such condition if it meets that threshold, that is to say if it establishes that, as a result, a claimant's life or safety would be jeopardized. This is in sharp contrast with undue hardship resulting from loss of employment, loss of status, reduction in quality of life, loss of aspirations, loss of beloved ones and frustration of one's wishes and expectations.16 The Court has reiterated the importance of not lowering that threshold.17

When asked by the RPD if there was any reason why she could not live in Accra, she only mentioned her fear of her husband:18 RPD: And are there any reasons...besides your husband and the fear that you have being kidnapped, is there any reason why you couldn't settle or move to Accra and live there, find work, find a place to live? Appellant: It's because my husband. RPD: Okay. Appellant: Because I am married to him and he owns me. He said if he does not have me, no one will have me.
The RPD found that it was not objectively unreasonable for the Appellant to live in Accra.

The RPD acknowledged that there is some level of discrimination against women in various aspects of life including housing, access to credit facilities and banking. In reviewing the Appellant's ability to reside in Accra the RPD found that it is likely not the norm for single women to live alone in Ghana; however, the documentary evidence does not indicate that she would not be able to secure housing as a single woman.19

With respect to the Appellant's personal circumstances the RPD found that the Appellant has travelled and lived away from home without issue, specifically she lived independently for five years in Ghana while attending school and successfully re-established herself in Winnipeg. Given her education in XXXXandXXXX XXXX, the RPD found that the Appellant has the skills and ability to find reasonably employment to financially support herself in Accra.

While recognizing the hardship in relocating to a new city and the Appellant's fear of her husband, considering the totality of the evidence the RPD found that relocating to Accra would not be objectively unreasonable.

The Appellant argues that being a single female, who has been married and is the survivor of domestic violence makes her more vulnerable than she was during the years in which she was working towards an education and living alone. The objective evidence20 cited by the Appellant reports on a 2015 survey of approximately 5,000 and summarized the key determinants of domestic violence as age (15-19-year-olds were more likely to experience) and exposure to violence in childhood, suggesting an intergenerational cycle. In addition to age, socio-economic factors were also found to be determinants of domestic violence. The summary does not identify the Appellant's profile as once married and a survivor of domestic violence as key determinants.

The Appellant also argues that her success in Winnipeg does not guarantee her success in Accra. The Appellant goes onto to argue that opportunities for women like her in Accra are limited and she would not have access to employment and resources to assist her healing from the trauma she had experienced.

The Appellant supports her argument with reference to objective evidence that women who experienced violence do not report their experiences due to cultural norms and have limited help.21 I note that in the objective evidence cited by the Appellant, an OECD report on the Social Institutions & Gender Index (SIGI) placed Ghana in the "Medium" category and assigned a value of 35%, where higher values indicate higher inequality, ranking it eighth among the countries in Africa.22 There is also objective evidence that mental health services are available in Accra.23
I do not find that the Appellant has provided any evidence to support her argument that she would not have access to employment or treatment in her particular circumstances.

The RPD made an observation about the Appellant's mental health; "her fear may impact her mental health, but it is speculative of the panel as to what impact her subjective fear may have."24 The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in making a determination about whether the Appellant's mental state allows her to be successful in the proposed IFA.

I note that the Appellant did not present any medical reports about her mental health. I find that, in the absence of such evidence, any observations or conclusions about her mental health by either the RPD or the Appellant are speculative.

The RPD took explicit account of the Gender Guideline,25 which requires consideration of gender in determining the ability of a woman to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without undue hardship. The RPD also noted that Ghanaian law provides from freedom of movement and the right to reside where they choose.26 I note also that Accra is serviced by an international airport27 facilitating the direct return and safe travel of the Appellant.

While relocating to Accra may be difficult for the Appellant, there is no evidence that the conditions would be unduly harsh. The Appellant may face the hardship associated with relocation and dislocation, but it is not the kind of hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.

For all of these reasons, I do not find that there is any "actual and concrete evidence" of conditions that would jeopardize the Appellant's life and safety in travelling or relocating to Accra. I find in all the circumstances, including circumstances particular to the Appellant, conditions in the proposed IFA are such that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellant to seek refuge there.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
